findings.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The wait_produce metric uses tag key "shards" while the produce and segment_size_bytes metrics use "shard" for the same joined shard string. Dashboards/alerts keyed on spans.buffer.flusher.produce{shard=...} silently miss the wait_produce series, which lands under a different tag key; whoever builds the per-shard flusher latency dashboard gets empty data for the produce-wait phase.

[ADVISORY] max_processes is computed with `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)`, so passing flusher_processes=0 (the only falsy int) silently degrades to one-process-per-shard instead of an error. An operator typo of --flusher-processes=0 (or an options value of 0) spawns one process per shard rather than failing loudly, the opposite of the intent of a cap, and only bites when shard counts are high enough to matter for resource usage.

[ADVISORY] The per-shard tag string (comma-joined shard list) is attached to the high-frequency spans.buffer.flusher.produce, segment_size_bytes, and wait_produce timers, creating unbounded metric tag cardinality as partition assignments change across rebalances. Metrics infrastructure operators get tag-cardinality growth with every rebalance (each new shard-set is a new tag value); the tag is a list, not a single shard id, so even a fixed cluster produces combinatorial values like '1,5,9,13'.

[BUG] The new --flusher-processes CLI option defaults to 1, silently changing default flusher behavior from one process per shard to a single process for all shards. On any deploy that doesn't explicitly pass --flusher-processes, max_processes = 1 (truthy, so `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` never kicks in) and every shard's flush work is serialized into one process — a throughput regression on the ingest-spans consumer path with no feature flag to revert it without a code deploy.

[BUG] The hang-restart path only kills processes that are instances of multiprocessing.Process, so in threading mode (produce_to_pipe set) the old un-killable thread keeps polling the same shards while a duplicate thread is spawned for them. When produce_to_pipe is set and a flusher is detected as hung, _ensure_processes_alive creates a second thread over the same shard list without stopping the first; both threads poll the same Redis shards, producing duplicate span payloads to Kafka and double-counting metrics. The `if not process: continue` guard at the top of the loop is also dead (dict values are always truthy objects), masking that this path was never exercised.

[BUG] Metric tag key is inconsistent: wait_produce uses tags={"shards": shard_tag} while produce and segment_size_bytes use tags={"shard": shard_tag}. Dashboards/alerts grouping spans.buffer.flusher.* by shard will split wait_produce into a separate tag dimension ('shards') from its sibling metrics ('shard'), breaking per-shard aggregation and alert queries on the touched metrics path.

[ADVISORY] _create_process_for_shard is dead code — no call site exists anywhere in the diff (restarts go through _create_process_for_shards), and its shard→process lookup duplicates the process_to_shards_map already consulted by the caller. The next maintainer changing restart semantics must reason about two near-identical restart entry points where only one works; the method restarts a process by scanning the map but ignores process_restarts bookkeeping, so any future caller gets unbounded restarts. Delete it.

[ADVISORY] join() shares a single deadline across sequential per-process wait loops, so the first slow process consumes the entire budget and all remaining processes are terminated while still alive. During consumer shutdown with a short timeout and multiple flusher processes, every process after the first is terminated mid-flush the moment its loop is entered, dropping in-flight segment flushes to Redis-backed loss and defeating the 'flush while next_step shuts down' design the comment describes.

[ADVISORY] The newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` intended to 'give flusher threads time to process after drift change' is a no-op because the same test monkeypatches time.sleep to `lambda _: None` at its start. The synchronization the comment claims to provide never happens; the test passes only by racing luck on thread scheduling, so it will flake (or silently stop covering the post-drift flush) for future maintainers who trust the comment. Call threading.Event or the unpatched time.sleep via a saved reference instead.

[ADVISORY] The new multi-process test only asserts process-count and shard-mapping bookkeeping; no test in the diff exercises the new multi-process runtime behaviors — _ensure_processes_alive restart/hang detection, the per-process backpressure raise, the >MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS RuntimeError, or that a limited-process flusher actually flushes data across shared shards. The concurrency and restart logic (the actual risk of this diff: shared self.stopped/current_drift Values across processes, per-process restart accounting, hang detection) ships with zero verification; a regression in _ensure_processes_alive only surfaces as unrecoverable consumer crashes or silent shard starvation in production. The existing test_flusher.py change only rewrites the old single-process backpressure assertion to the new dict shape.

[ADVISORY] This PR adds an unrelated documentation edit about hasattr() vs isinstance() for unions that has no connection to the stated intent of span buffer multiprocess enhancement with health monitoring. Reviewers and archaeologists tracing the flusher change get an untraceable doc change mixed in; a future revert or cherry-pick of the flusher work drags this hunk along (or vice versa).

[BUG] The new --flusher-processes option defaults to 1, silently changing the deployed default from one process per shard (previous num_processes = len(buffer.assigned_shards)) to a single flusher process handling all shards. On the next deploy without operator action, every shard's flush work is serialized into one process, reintroducing the exact throughput bottleneck this PR claims to fix — the stated intent is an enhancement, but the default ships a regression relative to current behavior.

[ADVISORY] The Redis memory check in submit() now iterates all per-shard SpansBuffer instances and calls get_memory_info() on each, multiplying the number of memory-info lookups per submit by the number of flusher buffers, and it does so even when only one buffer existed before. Operators running many shards see submit-path cost (and any backing service calls SpansBuffer.get_memory_info makes) multiplied by shard count on every submit, an unbounded hot-path cost that no requirement in this PR calls for.

[ADVISORY] _create_process_for_shard is dead code — no call site anywhere in the diff or existing code invokes it; restarts go through _create_process_for_shards directly. Its redundant shard-lookup loop invites a future maintainer to call it and get a duplicate process spawned for the shard's group without replacing the old one (since it calls _create_process_for_shards which overwrites self.processes[process_index] while the old process may still run), a change-safety hazard with zero present value; delete it.

[ADVISORY] In join(), the computed remaining_time is never used, and the sequential per-process wait loop means the timeout is not actually divided or propagated correctly — the `while process.is_alive() and (deadline is None or deadline > time.time())` guard silently ignores remaining_time. The variable is a misleading vestige; a reader assumes per-process timeout accounting exists when it doesn't (the shared deadline does bound it, but the dead variable obscures that), making the next timeout-related change riskier.

[ADVISORY] The new metric tag keys are inconsistent within the same loop body: flusher.produce and segment_size_bytes use tag key "shard" (singular) carrying a comma-joined shard list, while flusher.wait_produce uses "shards" (plural) — and flusher_unhealthy emits per-shard ints under "shard". Dashboards/alerts built on spans.buffer.flusher.* now have two different tag schemas for the same shard dimension (list-string vs individual values), so whoever builds the health-monitoring dashboards this PR's title promises gets fragmented series and must write per-metric special cases.

[ADVISORY] Each restart via _create_process_for_shards constructs a brand-new SpansBuffer(shards) and overwrites self.buffers[process_index], so the parent strategy's submit() immediately begins calling record_stored_segments on the new buffer while the freshly spawned process may not yet have registered its polling state — the optimistic-reset race the original comment warned about is now multiplied across per-process buffers. During frequent restarts (the exact unhealthy scenario this PR adds health monitoring for), transient duplicate record_stored_segments bookkeeping across old and new buffer objects can skew the drift/segment accounting used for commit decisions.

[BUG] A negative or zero `flusher_processes` value silently disables the flusher entirely instead of falling back to a sane default. `max_processes or len(...)` maps 0 to all-shards, but a negative CLI value (no validation on the click option) makes `num_processes = min(-1, len(shards))` negative, so `range(negative)` is empty: zero flusher processes are created, `process_to_shards_map` is empty, and segments accumulate in Redis forever with no unhealthy/restart detection to catch it — operators only discover it when Redis fills up.

[ADVISORY] The new metric tags use two different key spellings for the same dimension — `tags={"shard": shard_tag}` on `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `segment_size_bytes`, but `tags={"shards": shard_tag}` on `wait_produce`, and a per-int `tags={"shard": shard}` on `flusher_unhealthy`. Dashboards and alert queries built on one spelling silently miss the other series; the next engineer slicing flusher latency by shard gets an empty graph for wait_produce and has to rediscover the typo.

[ADVISORY] `_create_process_for_shard` is dead code with a latent double-start bug: it is called nowhere in the diff, and if a future caller invokes it, it spawns a replacement process without killing or joining the existing one for that process index. The next contributor who wires up per-shard restart (the name suggests that intent) gets two live processes flushing the same shards concurrently — duplicate segment production to Kafka — because the kill/terminate step present in `_ensure_processes_alive` is missing here.

[ADVISORY] The `remaining_time` variable computed in `join()` is assigned and never used, and the per-process wait loop after the `break` skips terminate for remaining processes only when the deadline fully expires while already-terminated processes are fine — the variable is a comprehension hazard. The next editor reading `remaining_time` assumes it bounds the inner loop (it does not — the inner while uses the raw `deadline`) and either adds logic on the wrong variable or removes the outer deadline entirely; the intended per-process timeout-budget accounting is not actually implemented.

[ADVISORY] The `shard_tag` metric tag is a comma-joined list of shard ids whose composition depends on each consumer instance's partition assignment, producing unbounded tag cardinality as assignments rebalance. With N shards distributed across consumers, the number of distinct `spans.buffer.flusher.produce{shard=...}` series grows combinatorially with assignment patterns; metrics infrastructure (and anyone aggregating by shard) gets tag explosion, and a rebalance silently forks every series into new tag values.

[ADVISORY] The flusher now constructs fresh `SpansBuffer(shards)` instances per process while the factory still passes the original whole-assignment `buffer` to the committer, so Redis-side buffer identity is split across two constructions of the same logical buffer. Any state added to `SpansBuffer` beyond pure shard-keyed Redis access (client-side caching, rate limiting, connection pooling assumptions) now has two divergent instance populations; the next maintainer adding instance state to SpansBuffer gets parent-buffer state that the flusher processes never see, and vice versa, with no compile-time or test signal.

[ADVISORY] When max_processes is None the flusher now defaults to one process per shard, silently changing the deployment topology for every non-CLI instantiation of the factory. Any deployment or embedding that constructs ProcessSpansStrategyFactory without the new --flusher-processes click option (other consumers, internal tooling, default SaaS config until the flag is explicitly set to 1) spawns len(assigned_shards) OS processes instead of the single flusher the original design guaranteed — a many-fold increase in spawned processes and Redis connections that no operator accepted. The click default of 1 papers over this only for the CLI path.

[BUG] join() breaks out of the per-process loop when the deadline expires, so processes after the current index never get terminate() called, leaving spawned flusher processes alive after the consumer shuts down. On a timeout-constrained shutdown with N flusher processes, the consumer main loop exits while some spawn processes keep running (their self.stopped is set, but the old code always called terminate() after the wait loop; here terminate is skipped entirely for the remaining dict entries). Leaked processes retain Redis connections and can keep producing to the pipe/topic after the consumer is considered joined.

[ADVISORY] Memory backpressure now sums used/available across one SpansBuffer per process-group, aggregating the same Redis service's memory stats once per shard-group instead of once per consumer. Operators using spans.buffer.max-memory-percentage get a used/available ratio computed from duplicated (or partially overlapping) ServiceMemory entries for the same Redis instance, skewing the backpressure threshold when flusher_processes > 1; with per-shard buffers each reporting the same service, the ratio itself is unchanged if entries are identical, but any per-shard scoping in get_memory_info makes the limit fire early or late depending on shard count.

[ADVISORY] New per-shard metric tags ('shard': shard_tag and 'shards': shard_tag) attach unbounded shard-combination strings to timers, and the two tag keys are inconsistent ('shard' vs 'shards'). Metrics infrastructure and dashboards built on spans.buffer.flusher.produce / wait_produce now see one series per shard-group (cardinality scaling with partition count), and the inconsistent key between the produce/segment-size tags ('shard') and wait_produce tag ('shards') means queries aggregating by shard silently miss the wait_produce timer; whoever maintains the dashboards gets bitten on the next partition rebalance.

[ADVISORY] _create_process_for_shard is dead code with no call sites anywhere in the diff. The next maintainer extending restart logic must decide between the dead single-shard entry point and the live _create_process_for_shards; leaving both invites a restart path that doesn't update self.buffers, so deletion is warranted.

[ADVISORY] The test's correctness now depends on a fixed time.sleep(0.1) to let flusher threads observe the drift change before join(), replacing the previously deterministic single-process behavior. On loaded CI runners the background thread may not poll Redis within 100ms, producing intermittent failures of the core consumer test — the reviewer who introduced multiprocess concurrency converted a deterministic test into a timing-dependent one without an acceptance note.

[BUG] An unvalidated --flusher-processes value of 0 (or negative) causes num_processes = min(max_processes, len(shards)) to be 0 or negative, and the round-robin assignment `i % self.num_processes` raises ZeroDivisionError (or negative modulo misassigns shards) at flusher construction, crashing the consumer at startup with an unhandled exception instead of a clean config error. An operator passing --flusher-processes=0 (easy typo, the click option has no validation) gets a ZeroDivisionError traceback at strategy construction; with a negative value, `min(-1, shards)` yields -1 and `i % -1 == 0` routes every shard to process 0, silently ignoring the intended limit and producing shard-to-process distribution nothing validates.

[BUG] The newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` in test_basic is a no-op because the same test monkeypatches `time.sleep` to `lambda _: None` at the top, so the comment 'Give flusher threads time to process after drift change' describes a wait that never happens. The test's claimed synchronization between the drift change and the flusher threads does not exist; any pass is due to incidental timing of `step.join()`, so the test is flaky-by-design and a future race in the drift handling would pass unnoticed.

[BUG] The rewritten per-process health monitoring and restart logic in `_ensure_processes_alive` (dead-process detection, hang detection via `process_healthy_since`, the per-shard `flusher_unhealthy` metric with cause tags, the `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS` RuntimeError, and kill/recreate of a single process) has no test in this diff that triggers any of its branches. I checked tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_consumer.py and tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_flusher.py — the only assertions touching this code are `len(flusher.processes) == 2` and the backpressure any() check; no test kills a flusher process or forces a healthy_since staleness, so a regression in restart logic (e.g. restarting the wrong process's shards, or never firing the RuntimeError guard) ships undetected to production consumers that must self-heal.

[ADVISORY] test_flusher_processes_limit verifies only internal bookkeeping (`flusher.processes`, `max_processes`, `num_processes`, shard-map totals) and never submits a message or asserts any segment is flushed through a shared-shard process. The core new behavior — that a single process correctly flushes multiple shards assigned to it via round-robin mapping — is unverified; a bug where the per-shard SpansBuffer passed to main() polls the wrong keys or drops shards would pass this test because it only counts structure. The rebuttal 'structure is all that changed' fails because `main()` now takes a `shards` list and uses shard-specific polling/metrics, which the test never executes end-to-end.

[ADVISORY] The changed `submit()` backpressure aggregation (iterating `process_backpressure_since` values) and the memory-check change (memory_infos now built from every per-shard buffer instead of one) are only covered by the weakened `assert any(x.value for x in flusher.process_backpressure_since.values())` in test_flusher.py, which cannot distinguish 'one process in backpressure' from 'all processes in backpressure' nor verify the MessageRejected raise. A regression where submit() ignores backpressure from a subset of processes (e.g. checking only the first one) still passes the existing test in the diff; the operator-facing consequence is silent Redis backlog growth on the unmonitored shards.

[ADVISORY] _create_process_for_shard is dead code — nothing in the diff calls it (restarts call _create_process_for_shards directly), and it also restarts by creating an additional process entry rather than replacing a dead one. Maintainers wiring shard-level restart into _ensure_processes_alive will hit a path that spawns a duplicate process for shards already owned by a live process, causing two flushers to concurrently read/claim the same Redis segments; whoever edits here next gets a riskier change because the two restart entry points look equivalent but are not.

[ADVISORY] The wait_produce timer uses tag key "shards" while every other metric in the same loop uses "shard", so the same dimension is emitted under two different tag names. Operators dashboarding on spans.buffer.flusher.* split by shard silently miss the wait_produce series; the typo is invisible until someone wonders why produce-time per shard exists but wait-time per shard does not.

[ADVISORY] join() breaks out of the per-process loop when the deadline expires, so any processes after the one being waited on never reach their terminate() call and leak. During consumer shutdown with a short join timeout and N flusher processes, up to N-1 spawn processes (holding Redis connections and producer futures with unflushed segment data) survive past shutdown; on consumer restart the same shards get a second live flusher, racing on Redis segment claims until the orphan exits.

[ADVISORY] On restart of a shared-process group, _create_process_for_shards replaces self.processes[process_index] and self.buffers[process_index] without killing a hung-but-alive threading.Thread path (isinstance check skips threads), and the old hung thread keeps polling the same shards' Redis segments concurrently with the new one. In the produce_to_pipe/thread configuration, a 'hang' restart spawns a second flusher for the same shards while the hung one still runs, producing duplicate Kafka messages for segments both claim and inflating restart counts; whoever debugs duplicate spans gets a race that only manifests after a hang-triggered restart.

[BUG] The health-check kill path skips terminating hung processes when produce_to_pipe is set (threading.Thread mode), leaking the hung thread while a replacement is started. In pipe/test mode, a flusher flagged with cause='hang' is never killed (`isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is False, and unlike the old code there is no ValueError-throwing kill on threads), so the stuck thread keeps polling its SpansBuffer while the new thread for the same shards also polls it — two flushers race over the same Redis keys, producing duplicated spans to Kafka and double-consuming segment state, and the hang is never actually remediated.

[ADVISORY] `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` treats the legitimate value 0 as absent, silently disabling the cap. An operator who sets --flusher-processes=0 (or any code path passing 0) to disable the flusher processes instead gets one process per shard — the maximum, not the minimum — with no warning; presence check `if max_processes is not None` would make 0 fail loudly or be rejected.

[ADVISORY] The `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` timer is tagged with key `shards` while every other metric in the same loop uses the key `shard`, splitting the same shard dimension across two tag names. Anyone dashboarding/alerting on `spans.buffer.flusher.*` by the `shard` tag gets no data for wait_produce (it aggregates under the orphaned `shards` tag), so produce-latency regressions per shard are invisible despite the diff's stated goal of per-shard observability; the divergence also means the existing test/monitoring conventions silently miss this series.

[ADVISORY] In submit(), the backpressure loop calls `metrics.incr("spans.buffer.flusher.backpressure")` once per unhealthy process before raising, so with N backpressured processes the counter is incremented N times per rejected message. The backpressure metric's rate is multiplied by the number of stuck processes, distorting dashboards that gauge how long or how often backpressure engages; operators correlating the metric with actual Kafka lag or Redis memory see inflated counts under the multi-process configuration this diff introduces.

[ADVISORY] `record_stored_segments()` and the memory-info loop iterate `self.buffers.values()` per submit() with no caching, and each SpansBuffer presumably issues its own Redis round-trips, so per-message Redis work is multiplied by flusher process count on the consumer hot path. A deployment with many shards and multiple flusher processes pays N× the Redis calls per submitted offset message (record + get_memory_info) where the pre-diff code made one set of calls; under load this raises consumer latency and Redis COGS proportionally to the shard/process fan-out, and the memory check's latency grows with process count on every submit when max-memory-percentage < 1.0.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The hang-restart path only kills processes that are instances of multiprocessing.Process, so in threading mode (produce_to_pipe set) the old un-killable thread keeps polling the same shards while a duplicate thread is spawned for them. adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] join() shares a single deadline across sequential per-process wait loops, so the first slow process consumes the entire budget and all remaining processes are terminated while still alive. As a result, if the first process consumes most/all of the timeout, subsequent processes will skip waiting because `deadline > time.time()` is already false, and then (for `multiprocessing.Process`) get `process.terminate()` immediately while still alive. This matches the finding’s shutdown/termination behavior for multiple flusher processes with short timeouts.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes memory backpressure computation in `SpanFlusher.submit` from a single buffer (`list(self.buffer.get_memory_info())`) to aggregating memory info across per-process/per-shard-group buffers (`for buffer in self.buffers.values(): memory_infos.extend(buffer.get_memory_info())`). Since the diff also introduces one `SpansBuffer(shards)` per process-group in `_create_process_for_shards`, this aggregation can plausibly include duplicated/overlapping `ServiceMemory` entries for the same underlying Redis service when `flusher_processes > 1`. The diff does not show any deduplication by service identity before summing `used` and `available`, so the concern is specific and grounded in the changed code, but whether `get_memory_info()` actually returns identical vs shard-scoped entries (and thus whether the ratio is skewed) is not verifiable from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] New per-shard metric tags ('shard': shard_tag and 'shards': shard_tag) attach unbounded shard-combination strings to timers, and the two tag keys are inconsistent ('shard' vs 'shards'). Metrics infrastructure and dashboards built on spans.buffer.flusher.produce / wait_produce now see one series per shard-group (cardinality scaling with partition count), and the inconsistent key between the produce/segment-size tags ('shard') and wait_produce tag ('shards') means queries aggregating by shard silently miss the wait_produce timer; whoever maintains the dashboards gets bitten on the next partition rebalance.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher.main`, the diff adds per-process shard tagging: `metrics.timer("spans.buffer.flusher.produce", tags={"shard": shard_tag})` and `metrics.timing("spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes", ..., tags={"shard": shard_tag})`, but `wait_produce` uses a different tag key: `metrics.timer("spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce", tags={"shards": shard_tag})`. This inconsistency is directly present in the diff and would cause dashboards/queries grouping or filtering by the `shard` tag to miss the `wait_produce` series. Also, `shard_tag` is a comma-joined list of shards handled by a process (e.g., multiple shards per process when `max_processes < len(assigned_shards)`), which creates a series per shard-combination rather than per shard, increasing metric cardinality with partition/shard layouts. This is an observability/metrics design issue rather than a functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] _create_process_for_shard is dead code with no call sites anywhere in the diff. The next maintainer extending restart logic must decide between the dead single-shard entry point and the live _create_process_for_shards; leaving both invites a restart path that doesn't update self.buffers, so deletion is warranted.

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, `SpanFlusher._create_process_for_shard(self, shard: int)` is newly added but is not referenced anywhere else in the shown changes (the live paths call `_create_processes()`, `_create_process_for_shards(...)`, and `_ensure_processes_alive()` which restarts via `_create_process_for_shards`). That makes it dead/unnecessary code in this PR, which is a maintainability concern rather than a functional defect. However, the finding’s claim that it could enable a restart path that “doesn't update `self.buffers`” is not supported by the diff: `_create_process_for_shard` delegates to `_create_process_for_shards`, which does update `self.buffers` via `_create_process_for_shards`/`_create_process_for_shards` -> `_create_process_for_shards` (ultimately `_create_process_for_shards` calls `_create_process_for_shards` which sets `self.buffers[process_index] = shard_buffer`).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The test's correctness now depends on a fixed time.sleep(0.1) to let flusher threads observe the drift change before join(), replacing the previously deterministic single-process behavior. On loaded CI runners the background thread may not poll Redis within 100ms, producing intermittent failures of the core consumer test — the reviewer who introduced multiprocess concurrency converted a deterministic test into a timing-dependent one without an acceptance note.

adjudication.rationale: In `test_basic`, the added `time.sleep(0.1)` does not actually sleep because the test earlier does `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`, patching the global `time.sleep` that the later call uses. So the test does not become dependent on “100ms” of waiting as the finding claims. While the added comment suggests a timing workaround, the diff shows it is a no-op in this test configuration, so the specific timing-dependence assertion is not verifiable from the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] An unvalidated --flusher-processes value of 0 (or negative) causes num_processes = min(max_processes, len(shards)) to be 0 or negative, and the round-robin assignment `i % self.num_processes` raises ZeroDivisionError (or negative modulo misassigns shards) at flusher construction, crashing the consumer at startup with an unhandled exception instead of a clean config error. An operator passing --flusher-processes=0 (easy typo, the click option has no validation) gets a ZeroDivisionError traceback at strategy construction; with a negative value, `min(-1, shards)` yields -1 and `i % -1 == 0` routes every shard to process 0, silently ignoring the intended limit and producing shard-to-process distribution nothing validates.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `--flusher-processes` as a plain `click.Option(..., type=int)` with no range validation, and wires it through `ProcessSpansStrategyFactory(..., flusher_processes=...)` into `SpanFlusher(max_processes=...)`. In `SpanFlusher.__init__`, `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` means a value of `0` will be treated as falsy and replaced by `len(buffer.assigned_shards)` (so the finding’s specific `ZeroDivisionError` for `0` is not supported by the code). However, a negative value (e.g. `-1`) is truthy, so `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(...))` can become negative. That makes `process_to_shards_map` empty (`range(self.num_processes)`), but the later round-robin assignment still does `process_index = i % self.num_processes` and then `self.process_to_shards_map[process_index].append(shard)`, which will raise at startup (likely `KeyError` for missing key 0 when `self.num_processes == -1`). This is an unhandled crash on bad operator input rather than a clean config error, so it’s a real defect exposed by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` in test_basic is a no-op because the same test monkeypatches `time.sleep` to `lambda _: None` at the top, so the comment 'Give flusher threads time to process after drift change' describes a wait that never happens. The test's claimed synchronization between the drift change and the flusher threads does not exist; any pass is due to incidental timing of `step.join()`, so the test is flaky-by-design and a future race in the drift handling would pass unnoticed.
matched_golden_ids: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate issue points out that test_basic monkeypatches time.sleep to a no-op (lambda _: None), so the later call to time.sleep(0.1) does not actually wait, undermining the intended synchronization. This is the same underlying problem described in the golden comment.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The rewritten per-process health monitoring and restart logic in `_ensure_processes_alive` (dead-process detection, hang detection via `process_healthy_since`, the per-shard `flusher_unhealthy` metric with cause tags, the `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS` RuntimeError, and kill/recreate of a single process) has no test in this diff that triggers any of its branches. I checked tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_consumer.py and tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_flusher.py — the only assertions touching this code are `len(flusher.processes) == 2` and the backpressure any() check; no test kills a flusher process or forces a healthy_since staleness, so a regression in restart logic (e.g. restarting the wrong process's shards, or never firing the RuntimeError guard) ships undetected to production consumers that must self-heal.

adjudication.rationale: The diff significantly rewrites flusher liveness/restart logic in `SpanFlusher._ensure_processes_alive` (per-process `process_healthy_since`/`process_backpressure_since`, exitcode vs hang detection, per-shard `spans.buffer.flusher_unhealthy` metrics, per-process restart counters and `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS` RuntimeError, and killing/recreating only the affected process via `_create_process_for_shards`). The added/updated tests (`test_flusher_processes_limit`, `test_basic`, and the backpressure assertion change in `test_flusher.py`) only assert process count/shard distribution and that some backpressure flag is set; none simulates a dead process (`is_alive() == False`), forces `process_healthy_since[...]` to become stale past `max-unhealthy-seconds`, or drives restart-limit behavior. So regressions in these new branches would not be caught by tests in this diff, which is a concrete, diff-grounded test gap rather than a proven runtime defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] test_flusher_processes_limit verifies only internal bookkeeping (`flusher.processes`, `max_processes`, `num_processes`, shard-map totals) and never submits a message or asserts any segment is flushed through a shared-shard process. The core new behavior — that a single process correctly flushes multiple shards assigned to it via round-robin mapping — is unverified; a bug where the per-shard SpansBuffer passed to main() polls the wrong keys or drops shards would pass this test because it only counts structure. The rebuttal 'structure is all that changed' fails because `main()` now takes a `shards` list and uses shard-specific polling/metrics, which the test never executes end-to-end.

adjudication.rationale: The new logic in `SpanFlusher` now partitions `buffer.assigned_shards` across `num_processes`, builds per-process `SpansBuffer(shards)`, and passes an explicit `shards: list[int]` into `main()` where flushing/metrics are shard-tagged (e.g., `_create_process_for_shards` creates `shard_buffer`, `main(buffer, shards, ...)`). However, the added test `test_flusher_processes_limit` only asserts internal structure (`len(flusher.processes)`, `max_processes`, `num_processes`, and shard-map totals) and then calls `step.join()` without submitting messages or asserting any flush/produce behavior for a process handling multiple shards. Therefore, a bug in the new multi-shard-per-process path (e.g., wrong shard keys polled by the per-process buffer) could slip through while this test still passes. This is a concrete, diff-grounded test-gap issue, not a directly verifiable functional defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The changed `submit()` backpressure aggregation (iterating `process_backpressure_since` values) and the memory-check change (memory_infos now built from every per-shard buffer instead of one) are only covered by the weakened `assert any(x.value for x in flusher.process_backpressure_since.values())` in test_flusher.py, which cannot distinguish 'one process in backpressure' from 'all processes in backpressure' nor verify the MessageRejected raise. A regression where submit() ignores backpressure from a subset of processes (e.g. checking only the first one) still passes the existing test in the diff; the operator-facing consequence is silent Redis backlog growth on the unmonitored shards.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces nontrivial behavioral changes in `SpanFlusher.submit()`: backpressure is now checked by iterating `self.process_backpressure_since.values()` and rejecting if any process exceeds the threshold, and the memory check now aggregates `memory_infos` across `self.buffers.values()` instead of a single `self.buffer`. The only related test adjustment shown is in `test_flusher.py`, changing `assert flusher.backpressure_since.value` to `assert any(x.value for x in flusher.process_backpressure_since.values())`, which does not exercise `submit()`’s `MessageRejected` path nor validate correct aggregation semantics across multiple processes (e.g., that backpressure in a non-first process is honored). This is a specific, diff-grounded test coverage gap rather than a demonstrated defect in the implementation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] _create_process_for_shard is dead code — nothing in the diff calls it (restarts call _create_process_for_shards directly), and it also restarts by creating an additional process entry rather than replacing a dead one. Maintainers wiring shard-level restart into _ensure_processes_alive will hit a path that spawns a duplicate process for shards already owned by a live process, causing two flushers to concurrently read/claim the same Redis segments; whoever edits here next gets a riskier change because the two restart entry points look equivalent but are not.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `SpanFlusher._create_process_for_shard`, but nothing in the shown changes calls it: startup uses `_create_processes()` -> `_create_process_for_shards(...)`, and restarts in `_ensure_processes_alive()` also call `_create_process_for_shards(...)` directly. So the “dead code” part is verifiable. Also, `_create_process_for_shard` would restart by calling `_create_process_for_shards` without stopping any existing process/thread for that `process_index`, and `_create_process_for_shards` overwrites `self.processes[process_index]` after starting a new worker, which would leave the old worker running but untracked (especially in the thread path where no `kill()` exists). That’s a concrete maintenance hazard created by the diff, even if it’s not exercised today.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The wait_produce timer uses tag key "shards" while every other metric in the same loop uses "shard", so the same dimension is emitted under two different tag names. Operators dashboarding on spans.buffer.flusher.* split by shard silently miss the wait_produce series; the typo is invisible until someone wonders why produce-time per shard exists but wait-time per shard does not.

adjudication.rationale: In src/sentry/spans/consumers/process/flusher.py, within SpanFlusher.main(), the produce timer and segment size metric use tags={"shard": shard_tag}, but the wait_produce timer uses tags={"shards": shard_tag}. This inconsistency will emit the same logical dimension under two different tag keys, making shard-split dashboards/alerts for spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce not line up with the other per-shard series. It doesn’t break runtime behavior, but it is a concrete, diff-grounded observability issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] join() breaks out of the per-process loop when the deadline expires, so any processes after the one being waited on never reach their terminate() call and leak. During consumer shutdown with a short join timeout and N flusher processes, up to N-1 spawn processes (holding Redis connections and producer futures with unflushed segment data) survive past shutdown; on consumer restart the same shards get a second live flusher, racing on Redis segment claims until the orphan exits.

adjudication.rationale: In SpanFlusher.join(), the loop over self.processes breaks entirely when the deadline has expired (`if remaining_time <= 0: break`). That means any processes later in the iteration are never reached and therefore never hit the `process.terminate()` call at the end of the loop. This is directly in the diff: `for process_index, process in self.processes.items(): ... if remaining_time <= 0: break ... if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process): process.terminate()`. So with a short timeout and multiple flusher processes, some processes can survive shutdown.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] On restart of a shared-process group, _create_process_for_shards replaces self.processes[process_index] and self.buffers[process_index] without killing a hung-but-alive threading.Thread path (isinstance check skips threads), and the old hung thread keeps polling the same shards' Redis segments concurrently with the new one. In the produce_to_pipe/thread configuration, a 'hang' restart spawns a second flusher for the same shards while the hung one still runs, producing duplicate Kafka messages for segments both claim and inflating restart counts; whoever debugs duplicate spans gets a race that only manifests after a hang-triggered restart.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher._ensure_processes_alive`, when a process group is deemed unhealthy (including the `hang` case), the restart path only attempts to kill the worker if `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`; for the `produce_to_pipe is not None` configuration, workers are created as `threading.Thread` in `_create_process_for_shards`, so they are never stopped/killed before `_create_process_for_shards` starts a replacement thread. Because the restart does not set `self.stopped` (only `join()` does) and the old thread remains alive, a hang-triggered restart can result in two threads concurrently running `SpanFlusher.main` for the same shard set (old `shard_buffer` + new `shard_buffer`), which can plausibly double-produce flushed segments for those shards.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The health-check kill path skips terminating hung processes when produce_to_pipe is set (threading.Thread mode), leaking the hung thread while a replacement is started. In pipe/test mode, a flusher flagged with cause='hang' is never killed (`isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is False, and unlike the old code there is no ValueError-throwing kill on threads), so the stuck thread keeps polling its SpansBuffer while the new thread for the same shards also polls it — two flushers race over the same Redis keys, producing duplicated spans to Kafka and double-consuming segment state, and the hang is never actually remediated.
matched_golden_ids: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate notes that in pipe/test mode a hung flusher is never killed because `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` evaluates to False, which matches the golden issue that spawn-created processes (SpawnProcess) on POSIX fail this isinstance check, preventing termination of hung processes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` treats the legitimate value 0 as absent, silently disabling the cap. An operator who sets --flusher-processes=0 (or any code path passing 0) to disable the flusher processes instead gets one process per shard — the maximum, not the minimum — with no warning; presence check `if max_processes is not None` would make 0 fail loudly or be rejected.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher.__init__`, the cap is set as `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)`. This treats `0` as falsy and replaces it with `len(buffer.assigned_shards)`, so passing `flusher_processes=0` (allowed by the new `click.Option(type=int)` with no validation) silently results in one process per shard rather than respecting the provided value or failing. A `None` check (or explicit validation rejecting 0) would avoid this behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` timer is tagged with key `shards` while every other metric in the same loop uses the key `shard`, splitting the same shard dimension across two tag names. Anyone dashboarding/alerting on `spans.buffer.flusher.*` by the `shard` tag gets no data for wait_produce (it aggregates under the orphaned `shards` tag), so produce-latency regressions per shard are invisible despite the diff's stated goal of per-shard observability; the divergence also means the existing test/monitoring conventions silently miss this series.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher.main`, the loop adds per-shard tags for other metrics using `tags={"shard": shard_tag}` (e.g. `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes`), but `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` is tagged with `tags={"shards": shard_tag}`. This is a concrete inconsistency introduced by the diff that will split the same dimension across two tag keys, making shard-filtered dashboards/alerts for `wait_produce` miss data when they expect `shard`. It’s observability/monitoring correctness rather than core runtime correctness.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] In submit(), the backpressure loop calls `metrics.incr("spans.buffer.flusher.backpressure")` once per unhealthy process before raising, so with N backpressured processes the counter is incremented N times per rejected message. The backpressure metric's rate is multiplied by the number of stuck processes, distorting dashboards that gauge how long or how often backpressure engages; operators correlating the metric with actual Kafka lag or Redis memory see inflated counts under the multi-process configuration this diff introduces.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher.submit()`, the code loops over `self.process_backpressure_since.values()` but calls `metrics.incr("spans.buffer.flusher.backpressure")` and then immediately `raise MessageRejected()` on the first process that exceeds the threshold. Because of the immediate raise, the counter is incremented at most once per rejected message, not once per unhealthy/backpressured process.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] `record_stored_segments()` and the memory-info loop iterate `self.buffers.values()` per submit() with no caching, and each SpansBuffer presumably issues its own Redis round-trips, so per-message Redis work is multiplied by flusher process count on the consumer hot path. A deployment with many shards and multiple flusher processes pays N× the Redis calls per submitted offset message (record + get_memory_info) where the pre-diff code made one set of calls; under load this raises consumer latency and Redis COGS proportionally to the shard/process fan-out, and the memory check's latency grows with process count on every submit when max-memory-percentage < 1.0.

adjudication.rationale: Diff shows SpanFlusher.submit() changed from single-buffer calls to iterating all per-process buffers: `for buffer in self.buffers.values(): buffer.record_stored_segments()` and, when `max_memory_percentage < 1.0`, it builds `memory_infos` by extending with `buffer.get_memory_info()` for every buffer. Since `self.buffers` is populated with one SpansBuffer per flusher process (`self.num_processes`), this makes the work in submit scale with flusher process count, whereas pre-diff it was a single `self.buffer.*` call. The finding’s performance/COGS concern is thus diff-grounded (even if the exact Redis round-trips per call aren’t provable from the diff).
